text: 1.1 Who are these guidelines for?
section_heading: 1.1 Who are these guidelines for?

text: These guidelines are for a person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU). In the lift industry, the PCBU is likely to be a company. In these guidelines, ‘you’ means the PCBU.
section_heading: 1.1 Who are these guidelines for?

text: The information is also relevant to workers in the lift industry. Workers can refer to these guidelines when planning or carrying out work, and when they are contributing to work health and safety decisions.
section_heading: 1.1 Who are these guidelines for?

text: These guidelines also include some information for building owners about their responsibilities under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 (HSWA).
section_heading: 1.1 Who are these guidelines for?

text: 1.2 What do these guidelines cover?
section_heading: 1.2 What do these guidelines cover?

text: These guidelines focus on work involving lifts, escalators or moving walkways. This work may include installation, servicing, maintenance, modernisation, decommissioning, and replacement.
section_heading: 1.2 What do these guidelines cover?

text: These guidelines do not cover temporary installations (such as construction site elevators), cable cars or passenger ropeways.
section_heading: 1.2 What do these guidelines cover?

section_heading: 2.1 What are key health and safety requirements to be aware of?

text: What are the duties of upstream PCBUs?
section_heading: What are the duties of upstream PCBUs?

text: A PCBU in the supply chain (upstream) also has a duty to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, that the work they do or the things they provide to other workplaces do not create health and safety risks.
section_heading: What are the duties of upstream PCBUs?

text: An upstream PCBU is a business that:
section_heading: What are the duties of upstream PCBUs?

text: – designs plant, substances, or structures
section_heading: What are the duties of upstream PCBUs?

text: – manufactures plant, substances, or structures
section_heading: What are the duties of upstream PCBUs?

text: – imports plant, substances, or structures
section_heading: What are the duties of upstream PCBUs?

text: – supplies plant, substances, or structures
section_heading: What are the duties of upstream PCBUs?

text: – installs, constructs or commissions plant or structures.
section_heading: What are the duties of upstream PCBUs?

text: Upstream PCBUs have additional duties (see Appendix 5). In the lift industry, upstream PCBUs include lift manufacturers and manufacturers of products used to fix and install lifts and escalators, such as solvents or degreasers.
section_heading: What are the duties of upstream PCBUs?

text: Upstream businesses are in a strong position to eliminate or minimise risk. They can influence and sometimes eliminate health and safety risks through designing, manufacturing, importing or supplying products that are safe for the end user.
section_heading: What are the duties of upstream PCBUs?

text: Good design, for example, can result in significant reductions in work-related ill- health and injuries, as well as enhancing the health, wellbeing and productivity of workers.
section_heading: What are the duties of upstream PCBUs?

text: A Health and Safety by Design approach focuses on the whole lifecycle. This means choosing safer and healthier options at every stage of a project, from the initial concept design through to decommissioning and disposal. It is often cheaper and more practicable to eliminate risks during the design or planning stage.
section_heading: What are the duties of upstream PCBUs?

text: What are overlapping duties?
section_heading: What are overlapping duties?

text: More than one PCBU can have a duty in relation to the same matter (overlapping duties). When you and other PCBUs have overlapping duties, this means that the duties are shared between you. This might happen in a shared place of work, such as an office building with multiple tenants where lift maintenance is being carried out.
section_heading: What are overlapping duties?

text: Example
section_heading: Example

text: A finance company leases a multi-storey office block from a building owner. Several lifts operate in the building. The building owner contracts Wrikerhen (a maintenance contractor) to maintain and repair the lifts.
section_heading: Example

text: PCBUs involved
section_heading: PCBUs involved

text: The building owner is a PCBU. The building owner manages and controls the building and has a duty to ensure people can safely enter and exit the building, and that the building is without risk to people.
section_heading: PCBUs involved

text: The finance company is a PCBU and has health and safety duties towards its workers and clients visiting its offices.
section_heading: PCBUs involved

text: Wrikerhen is a PCBU and has health and safety duties towards its workers and other people at its workplace.
section_heading: PCBUs involved

text: The PCBUs have overlapping duties
section_heading: The PCBUs have overlapping duties

text: The PCBUs have overlapping duties and must work together to ensure the safety of workers, other people in the workplace, and other people in the vicinity of any work carried out. The PCBUs must consult, coordinate and cooperate with each other to manage shared risks.
section_heading: The PCBUs have overlapping duties

text: The lifts in the building need to be maintained. Before lift maintenance begins, the building owner consults Wrikerhen and the finance company. This is so that all PCBUs know about the work and what they each need to do to ensure the safety of people in the building, including:
section_heading: The PCBUs have overlapping duties

text: – identifying the best time for the work to be done
section_heading: The PCBUs have overlapping duties

text: – putting up barriers around the work area and
section_heading: The PCBUs have overlapping duties

text: – discussing what information the finance company will give to its workers and clients.
section_heading: The PCBUs have overlapping duties

text: As the work proceeds, the finance company tells the building owner and Wrikerhen about any concerns or incidents so they can review them and make any changes needed.
section_heading: The PCBUs have overlapping duties

text: The finance company learns that Wrikerhen had not fixed a faulty barrier near the Level 5 meeting rooms, even though Wrikerhen had been told about it.
section_heading: The PCBUs have overlapping duties

text: As this faulty barrier could potentially harm clients:
section_heading: The PCBUs have overlapping duties

text: – workers were notified of the faulty barrier and told to use alternative lifts at the rear of the building
section_heading: The PCBUs have overlapping duties

text: – the finance company decided to hold all client meetings on the ground floor until the barrier was fixed.
section_heading: The PCBUs have overlapping duties

text: When can workers cease work?
section_heading: When can workers cease work?

text: A worker can stop or refuse to carry out work if they believe that the work would expose them or another person to a serious health and safety risk arising from immediate or imminent exposure to a hazard.
section_heading: When can workers cease work?

text: A worker who has stopped work must:
section_heading: When can workers cease work?

text: – as soon as possible, notify the PCBU that they have ceased work and
section_heading: When can workers cease work?

text: – remain available to carry out suitable alternative work.
section_heading: When can workers cease work?

text: WHAT IS ALTERNATIVE WORK?
section_heading: WHAT IS ALTERNATIVE WORK?

text: A PCBU can offer a worker alternative work until they can resume their normal duties. The work must be safe, appropriate for the worker to carry out, and within the scope of the worker’s employment agreement or contract.
section_heading: WHAT IS ALTERNATIVE WORK?

text: WHAT CAN YOUR HEALTH AND SAFETY REPRESENTATIVES DO?
section_heading: WHAT CAN YOUR HEALTH AND SAFETY REPRESENTATIVES DO?

text: A trained Health and Safety Representative (HSR) can direct a worker to cease work if they reasonably believe that carrying out the work would expose the worker, or any other person, to a serious health or safety risk.
section_heading: WHAT CAN YOUR HEALTH AND SAFETY REPRESENTATIVES DO?

text: The HSR must consult with the PCBU about the issue before giving the direction unless the risk is serious and immediate. In this case, the HSR can direct the worker to cease work immediately and consult afterwards.
section_heading: WHAT CAN YOUR HEALTH AND SAFETY REPRESENTATIVES DO?

text: For more information, see our guidance Ceasing work
section_heading: WHAT CAN YOUR HEALTH AND SAFETY REPRESENTATIVES DO?

text: 3.2 How can you manage the risks from working at height?
section_heading: 3.2 How can you manage the risks from working at height?

text: Workers can be seriously injured or die if they fall when working at height.
section_heading: 3.2 How can you manage the risks from working at height?

text: ‘Working at height’ means working in a place where a person is at risk of falling from one level to another. For example, work that takes place:
section_heading: 3.2 How can you manage the risks from working at height?

text: – above the ground level or floor level
section_heading: 3.2 How can you manage the risks from working at height?

text: – in an area where a worker could fall from an edge, through an opening, or through a fragile surface
section_heading: 3.2 How can you manage the risks from working at height?

text: – next to a hole or other opening at ground level.
section_heading: 3.2 How can you manage the risks from working at height?

text: What are the risks from lifting and rigging?
section_heading: What are the risks from lifting and rigging?

text: Lifting loads with rigging generally involves working with loads at height. Rigging refers to the use of mechanical load-shifting equipment and associated gear to move, place or secure a load.
section_heading: What are the risks from lifting and rigging?

text: Work that might involve lifting and rigging may include installation, major maintenance, refurbishment, decommissioning of a lift car within a lift shaft, lift motor room work (such as changing drive motors), and replacing lift ropes.
section_heading: What are the risks from lifting and rigging?

text: The main risks during lifting and rigging include, but are not limited to:
section_heading: What are the risks from lifting and rigging?

text: – workers falling from height and being harmed, and
section_heading: What are the risks from lifting and rigging?

text: – suspended loads falling and harming workers (see Section 3.3 of these guidelines).
section_heading: What are the risks from lifting and rigging?

text: How can you manage the risks?
section_heading: How can you manage the risks?

text: A combination of control measures may be needed. Control measures such as a safety harness will not prevent a fall, but they may minimise harm.
section_heading: How can you manage the risks?

text: ELIMINATING RISK
section_heading: ELIMINATING RISK

text: The most effective way to protect workers from the risk of falling is to eliminate the need to work at height.
section_heading: ELIMINATING RISK

text: Consider how the work could be carried out without exposing workers to the risk of falling. Elimination can often be achieved at the design, construction planning and tendering stages. For example, by building structures at ground level and lifting them into position when they are completed.
section_heading: ELIMINATING RISK

text: Make sure that any surfaces or materials that workers could walk on can:
section_heading: ELIMINATING RISK

text: – support a person’s weight, and
section_heading: ELIMINATING RISK

text: – can also support the weight of any equipment or materials the person may be carrying.
section_heading: ELIMINATING RISK

text: What could go wrong – working at height
section_heading: ELIMINATING RISK

text: Other control measures to manage the risk of a fall from height include:
section_heading: ELIMINATING RISK

text: – working from ground level using long-handled tools
section_heading: ELIMINATING RISK

text: – covering all holes or openings.
section_heading: ELIMINATING RISK

text: Identify and clearly mark access routes so that workers can avoid passing near fragile material such as glass or other surfaces that would not support their weight if they fell.
section_heading: ELIMINATING RISK

text: MINIMISING RISK
section_heading: MINIMISING RISK

text: If elimination is not practicable, then consider how to minimise the risk.
section_heading: MINIMISING RISK

text: ISOLATION
section_heading: ISOLATION

text: The risk of a fall can be reduced by using one or more of these control measures to isolate workers from the risk:
section_heading: ISOLATION

text: – edge protection, such as a guardrail system on top of a lift car
section_heading: ISOLATION

text: – a guard-railed work platform such as a scaffold (see scaffolding information below) or elevating work platform
section_heading: ISOLATION

text: – a barrier to restrict access (such as access to a lift shaft)
section_heading: ISOLATION

text: – a handrail
section_heading: ISOLATION

text: – a total restraint system (such as an anchored full-body harness) that prevents the worker from getting too close to an edge they could fall from.
section_heading: ISOLATION

text: MINIMISE THE DISTANCE AND IMPACT OF A FALL
section_heading: MINIMISE THE DISTANCE AND IMPACT OF A FALL

text: If elimination and isolation are not practicable, minimise the likelihood of harm resulting from a fall by using one or more of these control measures:
section_heading: MINIMISE THE DISTANCE AND IMPACT OF A FALL

text: – a fall arrest system designed to support and hold a worker if they fall
section_heading: MINIMISE THE DISTANCE AND IMPACT OF A FALL

text: – a work positioning system that uses a harness under tension to support the worker
section_heading: MINIMISE THE DISTANCE AND IMPACT OF A FALL

text: – a safety net or soft-landing system to minimise the distance and impact of a fall
section_heading: MINIMISE THE DISTANCE AND IMPACT OF A FALL

text: – an industrial rope access system.
section_heading: MINIMISE THE DISTANCE AND IMPACT OF A FALL

text: How can you manage the risks?
section_heading: How can you manage the risks?

text: – Regulation 24 of the GRWM Regulations specifies your duty to manage risks associated with working under raised objects.
section_heading: How can you manage the risks?

text: – Regulation 25 of the GRWM Regulations specifies your duty to manage risks associated with objects that are reasonably likely to fall on and injure a person.
section_heading: How can you manage the risks?

text: You must follow the prescribed risk management process described in our General risk and workplace management – Part 2 guidelines to manage these risks.
section_heading: How can you manage the risks?

text: You must first try to eliminate the risk so far as is reasonably practicable.
section_heading: How can you manage the risks?

text: – If you cannot eliminate the risk, you must minimise the risk by providing and maintaining a safe system of work that includes measures for preventing an object from falling freely so far as is reasonably practicable.
section_heading: How can you manage the risks?

text: – If it is not reasonably practicable to prevent the object from falling freely, use a system to arrest the fall so far as is reasonably practicable.
section_heading: How can you manage the risks?

text: If it is not reasonably practicable to prevent the object from falling freely or to use a system to arrest the fall, an exclusion zone that persons are prohibited from entering must be provided.

text: LOCKOUT AND TAGOUT PROCESS
section_heading: LOCKOUT AND TAGOUT PROCESS

text: Many workers in New Zealand have been killed or seriously injured when the machine they were servicing was turned on or restarted while they were working on it.
section_heading: LOCKOUT AND TAGOUT PROCESS

text: Machinery or other equipment that does not need to be operating should be:
section_heading: LOCKOUT AND TAGOUT PROCESS

text: – brought to a zero-energy state (completely de-energised), and
section_heading: LOCKOUT AND TAGOUT PROCESS

text: – locked out and tagged out from its power source(s).
section_heading: LOCKOUT AND TAGOUT PROCESS

text: Lockout
section_heading: Lockout

text: Lockout is the process of turning off machinery and applying a physical lockout device to its lockout point (for example, a disconnect switch, isolator switch, or circuit breaker). Types of lockout devices might also include padlocks, chains and hasps. More than one lockout device may be used to lock out machinery.
section_heading: Lockout

text: Tagout
section_heading: Tagout

text: Once machinery is locked out, it should be tagged out. This means a tag is attached to the machinery warning other workers that it is locked out and is not safe to use. Tags are sometimes called danger tags, restricted-use tags, or warning tags.
section_heading: Tagout

text: For a lockout to be safe and effective, it is critical to:
section_heading: Tagout

text: – shut down (isolate) all sources of energy to the machine, and
section_heading: Tagout

text: – release (de-energise) all the stored energy within the machine to prevent unplanned movement of machine parts that could cause injury.
section_heading: Tagout

text: You must make sure that workers who lock out and tag out machinery are trained in the correct procedure.
section_heading: Tagout

text: The lockout and tagout process is an administrative control measure, at the lower end of the hierarchy of control measures.
section_heading: Tagout

text: When you carry out a risk assessment, consider whether you can implement engineering control measures. Engineering control measures (such as interlocking guards) are higher in the hierarchy and considered to be more effective.
section_heading: Tagout

text: ASBESTOS-RELATED DISEASES
section_heading: ASBESTOS-RELATED DISEASES

text: Most asbestos-related diseases are caused by exposure to asbestos fibres at work. Even a small job like drilling a hole could expose a worker to danger.
section_heading: ASBESTOS-RELATED DISEASES

text: When asbestos or ACMs are disturbed or deteriorate, tiny asbestos fibres can be released.
section_heading: ASBESTOS-RELATED DISEASES

text: The risk to health is low if the asbestos or ACM is in good condition and undisturbed.
section_heading: ASBESTOS-RELATED DISEASES

text: SAFE WORK PRACTICES
section_heading: SAFE WORK PRACTICES

text: Workers should protect themselves against asbestos, even on small jobs that do not seem to create much dust. See Appendix 9 for examples of safe work practices.
section_heading: SAFE WORK PRACTICES

text: – If possible, plan the job so that no asbestos will be disturbed.
section_heading: SAFE WORK PRACTICES

text: – If asbestos has to be disturbed, do not start work until having the right information and training to work safely.
section_heading: SAFE WORK PRACTICES

text: Use the right PPE, such as suitable RPE. Not all masks will protect workers from asbestos – seek advice if unsure what type of RPE is suitable.
section_heading: SAFE WORK PRACTICES

text: Regulation 53 of the Health and Safety at Work (Asbestos) Regulations 2016 specifies how asbestos waste and contaminated PPE must be contained and disposed of.
section_heading: SAFE WORK PRACTICES

text: ADVICE FOR BUILDING OWNERS
section_heading: ADVICE FOR BUILDING OWNERS

text: Lifts, escalators and passenger walkways are under the control of the building owner. If the building owner knows – or can reasonably expect – that there is a risk of exposure to respirable asbestos fibres in their workplace, the building owner must make sure, so far as is reasonably practicable, that all asbestos or ACM is identified.
section_heading: ADVICE FOR BUILDING OWNERS

text: – The building owner must manage the risks if there is asbestos in any areas where workers will be working (for example, in the lift shaft).
section_heading: ADVICE FOR BUILDING OWNERS

text: – The building owner must confirm the condition of any asbestos that is identified. If the asbestos is friable and/or deteriorated, then it presents a risk. The risk must be managed so that maintenance or other work can be carried out safely. For example, a reasonably practicable step would be to remove any friable or deteriorated asbestos.
section_heading: ADVICE FOR BUILDING OWNERS

text: – The building owner must have a process for advising workers of any risks related to asbestos.
section_heading: ADVICE FOR BUILDING OWNERS

text: – Although it is the building owner’s duty to manage risks, the building owner is likely to ask the building management company to advise workers that the risks exist, and to explain how these risks will be managed.
section_heading: ADVICE FOR BUILDING OWNERS

text: – A property manager may arrange maintenance on behalf of the building owner.

text: RCDs
section_heading: RCDs

text: RCDs should be used with all portable tools and other electrical devices as required. All RCDs used to protect people should be rated nominally at 30ma or less.
section_heading: RCDs

text: An RCD constantly monitors the electric current flowing along a circuit. If an RCD detects a fault, it quickly disconnects the electricity supply in many situations where someone would otherwise receive a fatal electric shock.
section_heading: RCDs

text: An RCD provides a high level of personal protection. While RCD protection minimises the risk of serious electric shock, it does not eliminate that risk.
section_heading: RCDs

text: BATTERY-POWERED TOOLS OR EQUIPMENT
section_heading: BATTERY-POWERED TOOLS OR EQUIPMENT

text: Using battery-powered tools or equipment may minimise risks associated with a mains electricity supply. Faulty leads, faulty RCDs and operation in wet conditions can also put workers at risk.
section_heading: BATTERY-POWERED TOOLS OR EQUIPMENT

text: There is still a risk of electric shock from battery chargers that are plugged into the mains supply. Chargers are not weatherproof. They should only be used in a dry and dust-free environment.

text: section 22 of HSWA
section_heading: Appendix 2: So far as is reasonably practicable

text: Certain PCBU duties (the section 36–43 duties including the primary duty of care) must be carried out ‘so far as is reasonably practicable’.
section_heading: Appendix 2: So far as is reasonably practicable

text: What to consider when deciding what is ‘reasonably practicable’
section_heading: What to consider when deciding what is ‘reasonably practicable’

text: Just because something is possible to do, does not mean it is reasonably practicable in the circumstances.
section_heading: What to consider when deciding what is ‘reasonably practicable’

text: Consider:
section_heading: What to consider when deciding what is ‘reasonably practicable’

text: – What possible actions can be taken to ensure health and safety?
section_heading: What to consider when deciding what is ‘reasonably practicable’

text: – Of these possible actions, at a particular time, what is reasonable to do?
section_heading: What to consider when deciding what is ‘reasonably practicable’

text: Think about the following questions.
section_heading: What to consider when deciding what is ‘reasonably practicable’

text: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT THE RISK?
section_heading: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT THE RISK?

text: – How likely is the risk to occur?
section_heading: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT THE RISK?

text: – How severe is the illness or injury that might occur if something goes wrong?
section_heading: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT THE RISK?

text: – What is known, or should reasonably be known, about the risk?
section_heading: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT THE RISK?

text: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT POSSIBLE CONTROL MEASURES?
section_heading: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT POSSIBLE CONTROL MEASURES?

text: – What is known, or should reasonably be known, about the ways (control measures) to eliminate or minimise the risk?
section_heading: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT POSSIBLE CONTROL MEASURES?

text: – What control measures are available?
section_heading: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT POSSIBLE CONTROL MEASURES?

text: – How appropriate (suitable) are the control measures to manage the risk?
section_heading: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT POSSIBLE CONTROL MEASURES?

text: – What are the costs of these control measures?
section_heading: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT POSSIBLE CONTROL MEASURES?

text: – Are the costs grossly disproportionate to the risk? Cost must only be used as a reason to not do something when that cost is grossly out of proportion to the risk.
section_heading: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT POSSIBLE CONTROL MEASURES?

text: While PCBUs should check if there are widely used control measures for that risk (such as industry standards), they should always keep their specific circumstances in mind. A common industry practice might not be the most effective or appropriate control measure to use.
section_heading: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT POSSIBLE CONTROL MEASURES?

text: If PCBUs are not sure what control measures are appropriate, WorkSafe recommends getting advice from a suitably qualified and experienced health and safety professional.
section_heading: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT POSSIBLE CONTROL MEASURES?

text: For more information, see our guidance: Reasonably practicable
section_heading: WHAT IS KNOWN ABOUT POSSIBLE CONTROL MEASURES?

text: Appendix 3: Working with other PCBUs – overlapping duties section 34 of HSWA
section_heading: Appendix 3: Working with other PCBUs – overlapping duties section 34 of HSWA

text: More than one PCBU can have a duty in relation to the same matter. These PCBUs have overlapping duties – this means that the duties are shared between them.
section_heading: Appendix 3: Working with other PCBUs – overlapping duties section 34 of HSWA

text: Duties regularly overlap:
section_heading: Appendix 3: Working with other PCBUs – overlapping duties section 34 of HSWA

text: – in a shared workplace (for example, a building site or a port) where more than one business has control and influence over the work on site.
section_heading: Appendix 3: Working with other PCBUs – overlapping duties section 34 of HSWA

text: – in a contracting chain, where contractors and subcontractors provide services to a head contractor or client and do not necessarily share the same workplace.
section_heading: Appendix 3: Working with other PCBUs – overlapping duties section 34 of HSWA

text: A PCBU must, so far as is reasonably practicable, consult, cooperate and coordinate activities with all other PCBUs they share duties with so that all PCBUs can meet their joint responsibilities.
section_heading: Appendix 3: Working with other PCBUs – overlapping duties section 34 of HSWA

text: A PCBU cannot transfer or contract out of their duties, or pass liability to another person.
section_heading: Appendix 3: Working with other PCBUs – overlapping duties section 34 of HSWA

text: However a PCBU can make an agreement with another PCBU to fulfil specific duties. Even if this occurs, all PCBUs are still responsible for meeting their legal duties.
section_heading: Appendix 3: Working with other PCBUs – overlapping duties section 34 of HSWA

text: Example
section_heading: Example

text: A local hotel contracts out housekeeping services to an agency. The hotel and agency both have a duty to ensure the health and safety of the housekeeping workers, so far as is reasonably practicable. This includes the duty to provide first aid facilities.
section_heading: Example

text: The agency reaches an agreement with the hotel – if their workers need first aid while working at the hotel they can use the hotel’s first aid facilities.
section_heading: Example

text: For more information, see our guidance: Overlapping duties
section_heading: Example

text: Appendix 4: Worker engagement, participation and representation Part 3 of HSWA

text: Engage with workers and enable their participation
section_heading: Engage with workers and enable their participation

text: A PCBU has two main duties related to worker engagement and participation:
section_heading: Engage with workers and enable their participation

text: – to engage with workers on health and safety matters that affect or are likely to affect workers, so far as is reasonably practicable, and
section_heading: Engage with workers and enable their participation

text: – to have practices that give workers reasonable opportunities to participate effectively in the ongoing improvement of work health and safety.
section_heading: Engage with workers and enable their participation

text: A PCBU can engage with workers by:
section_heading: Engage with workers and enable their participation

text: – sharing information about health and safety matters so that workers are well-informed, know what is going on and can contribute to decision-making
section_heading: Engage with workers and enable their participation

text: – giving workers reasonable opportunities to have a say about health and safety matters
section_heading: Engage with workers and enable their participation

text: – listening to and considering what workers have to say at each step of the risk management process
section_heading: Engage with workers and enable their participation

text: – considering workers’ views when health and safety decisions are being made
section_heading: Engage with workers and enable their participation

text: – updating workers about what decisions have been made.
section_heading: Engage with workers and enable their participation

text: A PCBU must engage with workers during specified times, including when identifying hazards and assessing risks.
section_heading: Engage with workers and enable their participation

text: A PCBU must have clear, effective, and ongoing ways for workers to suggest improvements or raise concerns.
section_heading: Engage with workers and enable their participation

text: Appendix 5: Upstream duties sections 39–43 of HSWA
section_heading: Appendix 5: Upstream duties sections 39–43 of HSWA

text: A PCBU in the supply chain (upstream) also has a duty to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, that the work they do or the things they provide to other workplaces do not create health and safety risks.
section_heading: Appendix 5: Upstream duties sections 39–43 of HSWA

text: An upstream PCBU is a business that:
section_heading: Appendix 5: Upstream duties sections 39–43 of HSWA

text: – designs plant, substances, or structures
section_heading: Appendix 5: Upstream duties sections 39–43 of HSWA

text: – manufactures plant, substances, or structures
section_heading: Appendix 5: Upstream duties sections 39–43 of HSWA

text: – imports plant, substances, or structures
section_heading: Appendix 5: Upstream duties sections 39–43 of HSWA

text: – supplies plant, substances, or structures
section_heading: Appendix 5: Upstream duties sections 39–43 of HSWA

text: – installs, constructs or commissions plant or structures.
section_heading: Appendix 5: Upstream duties sections 39–43 of HSWA

text: Upstream businesses are in a strong position to eliminate or minimise risk. They can influence and sometimes eliminate health and safety risks through designing, manufacturing, importing or supplying products that are safe for the end user.
section_heading: Appendix 5: Upstream duties sections 39–43 of HSWA

text: Example
section_heading: Example

text: A worker using a badly designed or poorly manufactured saw may be at risk of injury. This risk should have been eliminated or minimised, so far as was reasonably practicable, by the designer or manufacturer.
section_heading: Example

text: Upstream duties for designers section 39 of HSWA
section_heading: Upstream duties for designers section 39 of HSWA

text: A designer creates or modifies a design for plant, substances or structures that are to be used or operated, or could be used or operated, in a workplace.
section_heading: Upstream duties for designers section 39 of HSWA

text: A designer has a duty, so far as is reasonably practicable:
section_heading: Upstream duties for designers section 39 of HSWA

text: – to make sure the products they design do not create health and safety risks for the people that use them and those nearby
section_heading: Upstream duties for designers section 39 of HSWA

text: – to make sure the products they design have been tested so they are safe for use in a workplace
section_heading: Upstream duties for designers section 39 of HSWA

text: – to give the following information to those who will use the designed products:
section_heading: Upstream duties for designers section 39 of HSWA

text: the design’s purpose or intended use
section_heading: Upstream duties for designers section 39 of HSWA

text: the results of any calculations or tests
section_heading: Upstream duties for designers section 39 of HSWA

text: - any general and current relevant information about how to safely use, handle, store, construct, inspect, clean, maintain, repair, or otherwise work near the designed products.
section_heading: Upstream duties for designers section 39 of HSWA

text: These requirements apply across the product’s entire lifecycle – from manufacture and construction, through to everyday use, decommissioning and disposal.
section_heading: Upstream duties for designers section 39 of HSWA

text: For more information, see our guidance: Health and safety duties for businesses that design products for workplaces
section_heading: Upstream duties for designers section 39 of HSWA

section_heading: Upstream duties for importers section 41 of HSWA

section_heading: Upstream duties for importers section 41 of HSWA

text: – that goods are imported for.

text: An importer has a duty, so far as is reasonably practicable:
section_heading: Upstream duties for importers section 41 of HSWA

text: – to make sure the products they import do not create health and safety risks for the people that use them and those nearby
section_heading: Upstream duties for importers section 41 of HSWA

text: – to make sure the products they import have been tested so they are safe for use in a workplace
section_heading: Upstream duties for importers section 41 of HSWA

section_heading: Upstream duties for importers section 41 of HSWA

text: A supplier has a duty, so far as is reasonably practicable:

text: – to make sure the products they supply do not create health and safety risks for the people that use them and those nearby
section_heading: Upstream duties for importers section 41 of HSWA

text: Upstream duties for installers, constructors or commissioners of plant or structures section 43 of HSWA
section_heading: Upstream duties for installers, constructors or commissioners of plant or structures section 43 of HSWA

text: An installer/constructor builds and/or assembles and installs plant and structures that may be used at a workplace. A commissioner performs adjustments, tests and inspections on plant and structures before they are used for the first time in a workplace.
section_heading: Upstream duties for installers, constructors or commissioners of plant or structures section 43 of HSWA

text: Appendix 6: Managing risk section 30 of HSWA
section_heading: Appendix 6: Managing risk section 30 of HSWA

text: This appendix describes a general approach to managing risk. Certain risks identified in these guidelines must be managed using a prescribed risk management approach. See the relevant sections for details.
section_heading: Appendix 6: Managing risk section 30 of HSWA

text: Risks to health and safety arise from people being exposed to a hazard (a source or cause of harm).
section_heading: Appendix 6: Managing risk section 30 of HSWA

text: A PCBU must first try to eliminate a risk if this is reasonably practicable. If it is not reasonably practicable to eliminate the risk, it must be minimised so far as is reasonably practicable.
section_heading: Appendix 6: Managing risk section 30 of HSWA

text: A PCBU must engage with workers and their representatives:
section_heading: Appendix 6: Managing risk section 30 of HSWA

text: – when identifying and assessing risks, and
section_heading: Appendix 6: Managing risk section 30 of HSWA

text: – when making decisions about how to eliminate or minimise the risks using appropriate control measures.
section_heading: Appendix 6: Managing risk section 30 of HSWA

text: Follow the steps below to identify, assess and manage work health and safety risks.
section_heading: Appendix 6: Managing risk section 30 of HSWA

text: STEP 1: IDENTIFY HAZARDS THAT COULD GIVE RISE TO WORK RISKS
section_heading: STEP 1: IDENTIFY HAZARDS THAT COULD GIVE RISE TO WORK RISKS

text: With your workers, identify what could harm the health or endanger the safety of one or more workers or others (such as visitors, or bystanders).
section_heading: STEP 1: IDENTIFY HAZARDS THAT COULD GIVE RISE TO WORK RISKS

text: STEP 2: ASSESS WORK RISKS
section_heading: STEP 2: ASSESS WORK RISKS

text: With your workers, identify and assess the risks arising from each work hazard. Ask:
section_heading: STEP 2: ASSESS WORK RISKS

text: – Who might be exposed to the hazard?
section_heading: STEP 2: ASSESS WORK RISKS

text: – What could happen?
section_heading: STEP 2: ASSESS WORK RISKS

text: - How severe could the resulting injuries be?
section_heading: STEP 2: ASSESS WORK RISKS

text: - How could people’s health be affected?
section_heading: STEP 2: ASSESS WORK RISKS

text: - How likely are these consequences?
section_heading: STEP 2: ASSESS WORK RISKS

text: Decide which risks to deal with immediately. For example, risks with potentially significant consequences such as serious injury or death, chronic ill-health, or those with a high likelihood of occurring.
section_heading: STEP 2: ASSESS WORK RISKS

text: STEP 3: DECIDE HOW TO MANAGE EACH RISK
section_heading: STEP 3: DECIDE HOW TO MANAGE EACH RISK

text: With your workers, decide how to manage work risks.
section_heading: STEP 3: DECIDE HOW TO MANAGE EACH RISK

text: Multiple control measures may be needed to deal with a given risk. Give preference to control measures that protect many workers at the same time (for example, safety barriers, safety nets).
section_heading: STEP 3: DECIDE HOW TO MANAGE EACH RISK

text: A PCBU can use the following hierarchy of control measures to work out the most effective control measures to use.
section_heading: STEP 3: DECIDE HOW TO MANAGE EACH RISK

text: Hierarchy of control measures
section_heading: Hierarchy of control measures

text: First try to eliminate
section_heading: First try to eliminate

text: First try to eliminate the risk, if this is reasonably practicable. This can be done by removing the source or cause of harm (such as faulty equipment, a noisy machine or a trip hazard).
section_heading: First try to eliminate

text: Then try to minimise
section_heading: Then try to minimise

text: If it is not reasonably practicable to eliminate the risk, the risk must be minimised so far as is reasonably practicable.
section_heading: Then try to minimise

text: Minimise the risk using one or more of the following actions:
section_heading: Then try to minimise

text: – substitute/swap with something that has a lower risk
section_heading: Then try to minimise

text: Most effective – isolate the hazard by separating people from the source of harm FIRST TRY ELIMINATION
section_heading: Then try to minimise

text: – apply engineering control measures (where physical components of the plant, Eliminate risks structure or work area are changed to reduce or eliminate exposure to hazards).
section_heading: Then try to minimise

text: IF ELIMINATION IS NOT REASONABLY PRACTICABLE If the risk still remains after taking one or more of the actions above, try to minimise the risk with administrative control measures (safe methods of work, Substitute Isolate Apply engineering control measures procedures or processes).
section_heading: Then try to minimise

text: IF THERE IS STILL RISK If there is still risk, use personal protective equipment (PPE) to minimise the risk. PPE is the least effective control measure, and should only be used when other Apply administrative control measures control measures alone cannot adequately manage the risk.
section_heading: Then try to minimise

text: STEP 4: PUT CONTROL MEASURES IN PLACE
section_heading: STEP 4: PUT CONTROL MEASURES IN PLACE

text: As soon as possible after a decision is made about the control measures, a PCBU should:
section_heading: STEP 4: PUT CONTROL MEASURES IN PLACE

text: – put the control measures in place
section_heading: STEP 4: PUT CONTROL MEASURES IN PLACE

text: – instruct and train workers (including new workers) about the control measures, including why it is important to use them and how to apply them.
section_heading: STEP 4: PUT CONTROL MEASURES IN PLACE

text: STEP 5: REVIEW AND IMPROVE CONTROL MEASURES
section_heading: STEP 5: REVIEW AND IMPROVE CONTROL MEASURES

text: Control measures should remain effective, be fit-for-purpose, be suitable for the nature and duration of the work, and be used correctly.
section_heading: STEP 5: REVIEW AND IMPROVE CONTROL MEASURES

text: With your workers, regularly monitor control measures to confirm that the measures are effective.
section_heading: STEP 5: REVIEW AND IMPROVE CONTROL MEASURES

text: You should review control measures:
section_heading: STEP 5: REVIEW AND IMPROVE CONTROL MEASURES

text: – when a new risk is identified
section_heading: STEP 5: REVIEW AND IMPROVE CONTROL MEASURES

text: – when there is a change at the workplace or to the work
section_heading: STEP 5: REVIEW AND IMPROVE CONTROL MEASURES

text: – when workers or their health and safety representative ask for a review
section_heading: STEP 5: REVIEW AND IMPROVE CONTROL MEASURES

text: – when there is evidence that control measures may not be working effectively to manage the risk (for example, when you receive monitoring results or a report following an incident investigation).
section_heading: STEP 5: REVIEW AND IMPROVE CONTROL MEASURES

text: Use guidance from WorkSafe or others (for example, industry associations) to help to identify, assess, and manage risks, and review control measures. If you need help, WorkSafe recommends getting advice from a suitably qualified and experienced health and safety professional.
section_heading: STEP 5: REVIEW AND IMPROVE CONTROL MEASURES

text: For more information, see our guidance: Identifying, assessing and managing work risks
section_heading: STEP 5: REVIEW AND IMPROVE CONTROL MEASURES

text: Appendix 9: Asbestos – recommended safe work practices
section_heading: Appendix 9: Asbestos – recommended safe work practices
